title: Boiled Plantains in their Skins
author: Laker Grace
desc: Medium-ripe plantains cut into four with the ends off but the skins left on, boiled hard fifteen minutes then simmered five, cooled and peeled at the table.
longDesc: Boiling plantains in their skins is the northern and eastern habit, and it does two useful things: the skin holds the flesh together so it does not break up, and it stops the plantain absorbing water. You cut the ends off and quarter them, skins on, put them in hot water, and boil hard before dropping to a simmer. They come out steaming hot, which is why the five minutes of cooling is written into the recipe rather than left to sense.
steps: Wash the plantains thoroughly with cold water.
Cut the ends off each one, then cut each into four pieces — leaving the skins on.
Put the plantains in a large saucepan.
Add hot boiling water to the pan.
Boil on high heat for 15 minutes, then reduce and simmer 5 minutes.
Let them cool at least 5 minutes — they will be steaming hot.
chefTips: Skins on. They hold the flesh together and keep it from waterlogging, and they come off easily once the plantain is cooked.
Cut the ends off first. It lets the heat in without letting the water into the flesh.
Start with hot water. Cold water means a longer climb to the boil and a softer result.
Fifteen minutes hard, five minutes gentle. The high boil cooks it; the simmer finishes it evenly.
Five minutes of cooling is in the recipe for a reason. Straight out of the pan these are genuinely too hot to peel.
Medium-ripe. Fully green is starchy and hard; fully ripe collapses.
They are good with anything saucy — stew, beans, spinach, peanut butter, groundnut sauce.
commonMistakes: Boiling gently throughout, so they never cook through.
Trying to peel them straight off the heat.
sources: Adapted from the boiled-plantains section of 'Ugandan African Feast', Amuna Foods (12 September 2021) — the quantities, the cut-the-ends-and-quarter-with-skins-on preparation, the hot-water start, the 15-minute boil plus 5-minute simmer, the 5-minute cooling and the peel-after-cooking order are as printed there.
The suggested accompaniments — stew, beans, spinach, peanut butter, binyewa or any other saucy food — are from the same source.
storage: Refrigerate up to 2 days, in their skins.
reheating: Steam for a few minutes, or fry the peeled pieces.
healthBenefits: Plantain is high in potassium, vitamin B6 and vitamin C.
Boiled in their skins with nothing added, so no fat at all.
A good source of resistant starch and fibre.
culturalNote: Boiling in the skin is one of those small regional differences worth noticing: in central Uganda matooke is peeled and steamed in leaves, while plantain boiled in its skin is more common further north and east. Same fruit family, two quite different plates.
